column4: In the parable, foam from both floodwater and smelted metal is cast away, while what benefits people remains on earth; this closely stages the section's distinction between lasting good and a fruitless yield.

The next verse contrasts those who respond to God and receive the best with those who refuse and face a bad reckoning and Hell; it supplies the moral outcomes after 13:17's image of what remains and what is discarded.
The person who seeks the immediate life receives only what is willed for him, while Hell is the end prepared for him; this directly asks what the seeker actually gets.
The one who seeks the Hereafter, strives for it with faith, has an effort that is appreciated; this is a specific counterpart to the section's successful search.
The following verse says that both groups receive provision from their Lord in this life, qualifying the idea of success by distinguishing immediate provision from the final outcome in 17:18–19.
The passage says the Hereafter is greater in rank and distinction than this life, directly extending the near-life versus lasting-good contrast in 87:16–17.
The worldly-life parable grows green, then dries and becomes scattered debris; beside the lasting good deeds of 18:46, it contrasts what vanishes with what remains.
The question about the greatest losers in deeds introduces people whose effort fails despite their confidence; the next verse supplies the section's specific parallel of a search that yields no good.
Their effort has gone astray in worldly life although they think they are doing well, a precise case of striving without attaining the sought good.
The next verse says their deeds are null and have no weight on the Day of Resurrection, completing the failed effort described in 18:104.
The verse states that wrongdoers are recompensed for their deeds and good-doers receive the best; it grounds the purification warning of 53:32 in the section's two different outcomes.
The passage singles out one who turns away; this gives a concrete act of avoidance alongside the section's account of the ashqa who avoids a reminder.
That person gives a little and then withholds, a specific image of the stinginess opposite the giving and purification in 92:18 and the self-sufficient course in 92:8.
Each soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow and to fear God; this makes the section's question of what each seeker gains an explicit self-accounting.
Those who forget God are made to forget themselves, a direct image of the self-neglect that the section calls dimming and diminishing the soul.
The continuation after the great fire of 87:12 says its inhabitants neither die nor live, completing the lasting consequence for the ashqa who avoids reminder.
Immediately after the division into wretched and happy in 11:105, the wretched are assigned to the Fire; the verse gives the first concrete outcome of the section's sh-q-w root.
The next verse describes their continued stay in the Fire, extending the wretched outcome from 11:106.
The happy are placed in the Garden and remain there; this completes the contrast introduced by the wretched and happy in 11:105 and makes lasting good concrete.
After confessing that their wretchedness overcame them in 23:106, the people ask to be taken out of the Fire so they can do good; the desired return is now unavailable.
They are told to remain there in humiliation and not speak, completing the failed plea of 23:107.
After the defiant tyrant has failed in 14:15, the next verse places Hell before him and describes a foul drink, giving that failure a concrete end.
The following verse depicts him barely swallowing, with death approaching from every side but not arriving; his striving ends in unrelieved affliction.
After 20:111 says the bearer of wrongdoing has failed, this verse gives the opposite case: a believer doing good need fear neither injustice nor loss.
The “tranquil soul” is a clear counter-image to the section's dimmed and diminished self.
The tranquil soul returns to its Lord both pleased and pleasing, giving the purified self a specific satisfied end.
The next verse invites that soul among God's servants, continuing its welcome after the return in 89:28.
The passage ends by admitting the soul to the Garden, the lasting good that contrasts with the section's failed outcome.
A believing man or woman who does good is promised a good life and reward according to the best of their work, concretely connecting good action with what the person receives.
The verse calls the one removed from the Fire and admitted to the Garden successful, defining success as the final outcome opposite to the wretched fire in the section's cross-references.
The righteous say they feed others only for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, a close parallel to 92:19–20's account of giving without seeking a return from people.
The righteous are told that their effort has been appreciated as their reward; this states the successful return to effort that the section contrasts with wasted toil.
